mcqs.question: In an unnormalized Enroll(student_id, student_name, course_id, course_title, instructor) table, why can't you add a brand-new course with zero students enrolled yet?
options: Because course_title is not allowed to be entered before instructor
Because student_id is part of the primary key and can't be NULL, so a row with no student can't be inserted
Because the database engine limits the number of courses per table
Because course_id must always be numeric
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic insertion anomaly: since student_id is part of the composite key, a row can't exist without a student value, so a course with no enrolled students has nowhere to be recorded. There's no such ordering rule, no course-count limit, and no numeric-only restriction implied here.

mcqs.question: A table's key is course_id, and it has an attribute chain course_id -> instructor -> office_number. What normal form does this violate?
options: 1NF, because office_number is a repeating group
This violates no normal form since the key still determines everything eventually
2NF, because office_number depends on only part of a composite key
3NF, because office_number transitively depends on course_id through the non-key attribute instructor
mcqs.explanation: office_number depends on instructor, which is itself a non-key attribute depending on the key — a transitive dependency, which is exactly the 3NF violation. It isn't a repeating group (1NF), and 2NF's partial-dependency issue only applies to composite keys, which this single-column key isn't.

mcqs.question: In Bookings(student_id, course_id, instructor) where {student_id, course_id} is the key and each instructor teaches exactly one course (instructor -> course_id), why does this table pass 3NF but fail BCNF?
options: Because course_id is part of the primary key, so 3NF's carve-out for key-part determinants applies, but BCNF has no such carve-out
Because 3NF doesn't check functional dependencies at all
Because instructor is not a real attribute of the table
Because BCNF only applies to tables with a single-column key
mcqs.explanation: 3NF allows a non-key determinant (instructor) if what it determines (course_id) is part of a candidate key — exactly this table's situation. BCNF removes that carve-out entirely, requiring instructor itself to be a superkey, which it isn't. 3NF does check FDs; instructor is a genuine attribute; BCNF applies regardless of whether a key is composite or single-column.

mcqs.question: What is the key practical trade-off between normalizing to 3NF versus pushing further to BCNF?
options: BCNF always uses less storage but is slower to query than 3NF
There is no real difference; BCNF and 3NF always produce identical decompositions
3NF cannot eliminate any redundancy at all, while BCNF eliminates all of it
3NF always preserves the ability to check every original functional dependency without a join; some BCNF decompositions lose that dependency-preservation property
mcqs.explanation: The real trade-off is dependency preservation: 3NF decompositions can always preserve the ability to verify original FDs without a join, while some BCNF decompositions can't. 3NF does eliminate most redundancy (just not all, unlike the claim here), and BCNF/3NF decompositions frequently differ.

mcqs.question: What makes a decomposition of table R into R1 and R2 'lossless' rather than 'lossy'?
options: R1 and R2 must each have fewer columns than the original R
R1 and R2 together must contain every attribute that was in R, in any arrangement
The common attributes between R1 and R2 (R1 intersect R2) must form a superkey of at least one of them
R1 and R2 must be exactly the same size in row count
mcqs.explanation: The lossless-join test specifically requires the shared attributes to be a superkey of at least one of the two decomposed tables — that's what guarantees rejoining reconstructs exactly the original rows, no more and no fewer. Column count, row-count parity, and simply covering all original attributes don't by themselves prevent spurious tuples on rejoin.

mcqs.question: Bookings(guest_name, room_number, room_type) is split into T1(guest_name, room_type) and T2(room_number, room_type) to remove a dependency involving room_type. Many rooms share the same room_type, and room_type is not a key of either table. What's the risk?
options: None — removing a bad functional dependency always produces a safe decomposition
The decomposition is safe as long as both tables have the same number of rows
Joining T1 and T2 back on room_type can produce guest-room combinations that were never actually booked, since room_type isn't a superkey of either table
T1 and T2 can never be joined back together at all after this split
mcqs.explanation: Since room_type isn't a superkey of either T1 or T2, the lossless-join test fails, and rejoining on room_type can fabricate guest-room pairings that never existed — a lossy decomposition. Removing a bad FD doesn't automatically guarantee losslessness; equal row counts don't ensure it either; and the tables absolutely can still be joined, just incorrectly.
